items.title: Home
items.text: LuaCord lets you write plugins for Spigot and Paper servers in Lua instead of Java. Lua is small and friendly, so you can go from nothing to a working plugin in a few minutes, and a plugin can be as simple as a single file.

items.title: Why LuaCord?
items.text:
LuaCord plugins are real plugins, so you get commands, events, permissions and config files, and the whole Spigot API is available from Lua. When you're ready to share your work, you can pack it as a .jar and upload it to CurseForge or Modrinth.

Start here

items.title: LuaCord and Lukkit
items.text:
LuaCord is a fork of Lukkit, originally created by jammehcow and others. Lukkit is archived and no longer updated, so LuaCord carries it forward: it works on modern servers, and existing Lukkit plugins should keep working.

This wiki is still growing, so until it catches up the old Lukkit wiki is still worth a look. It's very old, but most of it still works with LuaCord.

items.title: The LuaCord website
items.text: The main LuaCord website, luacordmc.github.io, has the download links for CurseForge and Modrinth, and the JAR generator.

items.title: Basics
items.text:
By now you've made a few plugins, so Basics is where you learn how to make them do more. It covers the things nearly every plugin needs, and it also shows you how to find everything else on your own, because Spigot is far too big for any wiki to cover in full.

Each topic works like your first plugin did. We build something one part at a time, explain each part as we go, and put it all together into one working plugin at the end. The topics build on each other, so it's best to go in order.

items.title: Commands
items.text: You'll learn how to read what a player types after a command, how to tell a player from the console, and how to reply with a helpful message. You'll finish with a /heal that works from the console too and can heal other players.

items.title: Events
items.text: You'll learn how to see what an event gives you and how to cancel one so the thing never happens. You'll finish with a plugin that stops players from breaking certain blocks.

items.title: Messages and colors
items.text: You'll learn how to add color to messages and how to send one to a single player or to everyone on the server. You'll finish with an announcement command that broadcasts a colorful message.

items.title: Working with players
items.text: You'll learn how to find a player by name and how to change things about them, like their game mode or where they are. You'll finish with a few handy admin commands.

items.title: Reading the Spigot docs
items.text: You'll learn how to open the Spigot documentation, find the thing you need, read what it expects, and turn it into Lua. You'll finish by using a method you looked up yourself.

items.title: Config files
items.text: You'll learn how to keep settings in a config.yml that the server owner can edit, and how to set defaults and read values. You'll also learn how to update an old config when your plugin changes, so server owners don't lose their settings. You'll finish with a welcome plugin whose message can be changed without touching any code.

items.title: Saving data
items.text: You'll learn how to save your plugin's own data to a file so it's still there after a restart, and how to update old saved data when your plugin changes. You'll finish with a plugin that remembers how many times each player has joined.

items.title: Commands
items.text: Commands are how players talk to your plugin, so almost every plugin has some. You've already made a few, but none of them cared about what the player typed after the command. In this lesson you'll learn to read that, and you'll finish with a /heal that can heal you, heal another player, and even work from the console.

items.title: Part 1: Read what the player typed
items.text:
Everything typed after the command name is called the arguments. Try this command to see them:

main.lua
plugin.addCommand({
    name = "echo",
    description = "Show what you typed",
    usage = "/echo <words>"
}, function(event)
    local sender = event.getSender()
    local args = event.getArgs()
    sender:sendMessage("You typed " .. #args .. " word(s).")
    sender:sendMessage("The first word was: " .. tostring(args[1]))
end)

event.getArgs() gives you the arguments as a list with one word in each spot. If someone types /echo hello there, the list holds hello and there. Putting # in front of the list counts how many words it holds, and args[1] is the first word, because Lua starts counting at 1 instead of 0.

If the player types nothing, args[1] is nil, which is Lua's way of saying "there's nothing here". The tostring part turns nil into text, so the message can still be sent.

Try /echo hello there and then just /echo to see both cases.

items.title: Part 2: Player or console?
items.text:
Commands can be run by players, by the console, and by command blocks, so it's worth knowing who you're dealing with:

main.lua
plugin.addCommand({
    name = "whoami",
    description = "Tell me who ran this command",
    usage = "/whoami"
}, function(event)
    local sender = event.getSender()
    if event.isPlayerSender() then
        sender:sendMessage("You are a player.")
    else
        sender:sendMessage("You are not a player, so you're probably the console.")
    end
end)

event.isPlayerSender() is true when a player ran the command and false otherwise. This is why the /heal from earlier didn't work in the console: the console isn't a player, so it has no health to fill. Try /whoami in game and then from the server console.

items.title: Part 3: Find another player
items.text:
To act on a different player, you need to look them up by name:

main.lua
plugin.addCommand({
    name = "isonline",
    description = "Check if a player is online",
    usage = "/isonline <player>",
    minArgs = 1,
    maxArgs = 1
}, function(event)
    local sender = event.getSender()
    local args = event.getArgs()
    local target = plugin.getServer():getPlayer(args[1])
    if target then
        sender:sendMessage(target:getName() .. " is online!")
    else
        sender:sendMessage("That player isn't online.")
    end
end)

plugin.getServer() gives you the server, and :getPlayer(name) looks for an online player with that name. If it finds one you get the player, and if not you get nil. That's why if target then works: a player counts as "yes" and nil counts as "no".

minArgs = 1 and maxArgs = 1 tell LuaCord to check the number of arguments for you. If someone types /isonline with no name, or with two names, LuaCord replies with an error message and your function never runs.

Dot or colon, again

plugin.getServer() uses a dot because plugin belongs to LuaCord. Then :getPlayer(...) uses a colon, because the server comes from Spigot.

items.title: Putting it together
items.text:
Now let's use all three to make a better /heal. Replace your old one with this:

main.lua
plugin.addCommand({
    name = "heal",
    description = "Heal yourself or another player",
    usage = "/heal [player]",
    maxArgs = 1
}, function(event)
    local sender = event.getSender()
    local args = event.getArgs()
    local target = nil

    if args[1] then
        target = plugin.getServer():getPlayer(args[1])
    elseif event.isPlayerSender() then
        target = sender
    end

    if target then
        target:setHealth(20)
        target:sendMessage("You were healed!")
    else
        sender:sendMessage("Couldn't find anyone to heal. Use /heal <player>.")
    end
end)

target is the player we're going to heal, and it starts as nil, which means we haven't picked anyone yet. The first if fills it in. If a name was typed, we look that player up, and if nobody by that name is online it stays nil. If no name was typed and a player ran the command, the target is the sender, so they heal themselves. If no name was typed and it's the console, nobody is picked, so it stays nil there too.

The second if then checks whether we found anyone. If we did, we heal them and tell them. If not, we explain how to use the command.

Try these, and watch what comes back each time:

  • /heal in game heals you.
  • /heal Steve, with a real player's name, heals them.
  • /heal Nobody says it couldn't find anyone.
  • /heal in the console says it couldn't find anyone, since the console isn't a player.
  • /heal Steve in the console works.
  • /heal a b gets LuaCord's too many arguments error.

items.title: Command options
items.text:
This is everything you can put in the table you give to plugin.addCommand. You always need name and description, and the rest are optional.

Option What it does Example name What players type after the slash name = "heal" description A short summary of the command. Without one, the command won't register. description = "Heal a player" usage How to use the command usage = "/heal [player]" permission Only people with this permission can use the command permission = "myplugin.heal" minArgs The fewest arguments allowed. LuaCord shows an error if there are fewer. minArgs = 1 maxArgs The most arguments allowed. LuaCord shows an error if there are more. maxArgs = 1 runAsync Runs the command in the background. Most Spigot actions aren't safe there, so leave this off for now. runAsync = false

items.title: What the event gives you
items.text:
Your command function looks like function(event), and this is what you can call on that event.

Call What you get Example event.getSender() Whoever ran the command. See everything you can do with it. local sender = event.getSender() event.getArgs() A list of the words typed after the command local args = event.getArgs() event.getCommand() The name of the command that was used event.getCommand() event.isPlayerSender() true if a player ran it if event.isPlayerSender() then event.isConsoleSender() true if the console ran it if event.isConsoleSender() then event.isBlockSender() true if a command block ran it if event.isBlockSender() then event.isEntitySender() true if an entity ran it, and players count as entities if event.isEntitySender() then

Next up is events.

items.title: Config files
items.text: A config file lets the person running the server change how your plugin behaves without touching any code. In this lesson you'll learn how to create settings with defaults, read them, change them from code, and update an old config when your plugin changes. You'll finish with a welcome plugin whose message can be changed without opening main.lua.

items.title: Part 1: Create settings with defaults
items.text:
A setting is a name and a value. The name is something like welcome-message, and the value can be text, a number, or true or false. Add this to your main.lua:

main.lua
plugin.onEnable(function()
    config.setDefault("welcome-message", "&aWelcome to the server, {player}!")
    config.setDefault("welcome-enabled", true)
    config.save()
end)

config is always there in your code, like plugin, and it's the place for everything to do with your config file. config.setDefault creates a setting, but only if it doesn't exist yet. That matters, because the next time the server starts, it won't overwrite a value that someone has changed. Then config.save() writes everything to the file. LuaCord doesn't save on its own, so without that line, no file appears.

Restart the server, then look in plugins/ for a folder named after your plugin, which is the name in your plugin.yml. Inside is a file called config.yml, and it looks something like this:

config.yml
welcome-message: '&aWelcome to the server, {player}!'
welcome-enabled: true

This is the file the server owner edits. The {player} part is a placeholder, and in the next part your code will swap it for the player's name.

items.title: Another way: ship a config file
items.text:
Instead of setDefault, you can include a ready-made config.yml in your plugin. Create a file called config.yml in the same folder as main.lua and plugin.yml, and write your settings in it:

config.yml
welcome-message: "&aWelcome to the server, {player}!"
welcome-enabled: true

Your plugin then looks like this:

MyPlugin.lkt/
├── config.yml
├── main.lua
└── plugin.yml

If you pack your plugin as a .lkt file, put config.yml at the top, next to main.lua.

The first time the plugin loads, LuaCord checks whether there's a config file in plugins/YourPluginName/ yet. If there isn't, it copies yours there, and from then on your code can read settings straight away with config.getValue("welcome-message"), with no setDefault needed.

The catch is that it's only copied once. If you add a new setting to your config.yml later, servers that already have a config won't get it, because their file is never replaced. That's why setDefault is usually the better choice, since it adds any missing setting every time the plugin starts. You can also use both: ship a config.yml, and add a setDefault line for anything you add later.

items.title: Part 2: Read a setting
items.text:
Now let's use the settings. Replace your join event with this one, along with the color helper from the Messages lesson:

main.lua
local function color(text)
    return (text:gsub("&", "\194\167"))
end

plugin.registerEvent("PlayerJoinEvent", function(event)
    if config.getValue("welcome-enabled") then
        local player = event:getPlayer()
        local message = config.getValue("welcome-message")
        message = message:gsub("{player}", player:getName())
        player:sendMessage(color(message))
    end
end)

config.getValue("welcome-enabled") gives back the value of that setting. It's true or false, so it works directly in an if, and the welcome only happens when it's true. Then config.getValue("welcome-message") gives back the text. After that comes message = message:gsub("{player}", player:getName()), which is the same gsub tool the color helper used in the Messages lesson. It means "replace every this with that", so here it replaces {player} with the player's real name. If the message is Welcome, {player}! and the player is Steve, it becomes Welcome, Steve!. We save the result back into message, so the next line uses the updated text. (gsub also reports how many swaps it made, but saving it into one variable keeps just the text.)

Finally, color turns the & codes into colors.

Because setDefault ran when the plugin started, these settings always exist by the time a player joins.

Try it by joining, then open config.yml and change the message. Settings are only read when the plugin loads, so restart the server (or reload the plugin) and join again.

A missing setting isn't nil

If you ask config.getValue for a setting that doesn't exist, you don't get nil. You get something that looks like a value, so if config.getValue("typo") then is always true. Make sure every setting has a setDefault, and double-check the spelling of the names.

items.title: Part 3: Change a setting from code
items.text:
Sometimes you want the plugin itself to change a setting, like an admin command. Here's one that changes the welcome message from inside the game:

main.lua
plugin.addCommand({
    name = "setwelcome",
    description = "Change the welcome message",
    usage = "/setwelcome <message>",
    permission = "welcome.set",
    minArgs = 1
}, function(event)
    local sender = event.getSender()
    local message = table.concat(event.getArgs(), " ")

    config.set("welcome-message", message)
    config.save()
    sender:sendMessage("Welcome message updated!")
end)

config.set changes a setting to a new value, whether or not it existed before. That's the difference from setDefault, which only fills in a setting that's missing. As before, config.save() writes the change to the file, so it survives a restart.

Try /setwelcome &bHello, {player}!, then join the server again.

items.title: Part 4: Update an old config
items.text:
Your plugin will change over time, and the server owners who already have a config.yml shouldn't lose their settings when you update it.

Adding a new setting is easy. Add another config.setDefault line to your plugin. Existing owners keep every value they've already changed, and they get the new setting filled in with its default the next time the server starts. Their file is never replaced.

Renaming a setting takes a bit more care. Say an old version of your plugin called it welcome, and you want to rename it to welcome-message without losing what people wrote. To do that, keep a version number in the config and move the value once:

main.lua
plugin.onEnable(function()
    config.setDefault("config-version", 1)

    -- Version 2 renamed "welcome" to "welcome-message"
    if config.getValue("config-version") < 2 then
        local oldMessage = config.getValue("welcome")
        if type(oldMessage) == "string" then
            config.set("welcome-message", oldMessage)
            config.clear("welcome")
        end
        config.set("config-version", 2)
    end

    config.setDefault("welcome-message", "&aWelcome to the server, {player}!")
    config.setDefault("welcome-enabled", true)
    config.save()
end)

An old config has no config-version, so it starts at 1 and goes into the if. There, we check whether the old welcome setting holds text. We check for text with type(oldMessage) == "string" instead of a plain if, because of the warning in Part 2. If it does, we copy it into welcome-message, remove the old one with config.clear, and mark the config as version 2. A brand new config has no welcome setting, so it skips the copy and just gets the defaults.

Next time you rename something, bump the number and add another if for it.

items.title: Putting it together
items.text:
Combined, your main.lua is a welcome plugin whose message can be changed in the config file, or with a command:

main.lua
local function color(text)
    return (text:gsub("&", "\194\167"))
end

plugin.onEnable(function()
    config.setDefault("welcome-message", "&aWelcome to the server, {player}!")
    config.setDefault("welcome-enabled", true)
    config.save()
end)

plugin.registerEvent("PlayerJoinEvent", function(event)
    if config.getValue("welcome-enabled") then
        local player = event:getPlayer()
        local message = config.getValue("welcome-message")
        message = message:gsub("{player}", player:getName())
        player:sendMessage(color(message))
    end
end)

plugin.addCommand({
    name = "setwelcome",
    description = "Change the welcome message",
    usage = "/setwelcome <message>",
    permission = "welcome.set",
    minArgs = 1
}, function(event)
    local sender = event.getSender()
    local message = table.concat(event.getArgs(), " ")

    config.set("welcome-message", message)
    config.save()
    sender:sendMessage("Welcome message updated!")
end)

Try these:

  • Join the server and see the welcome message.
  • Change welcome-message in config.yml, restart, and join again.
  • Set welcome-enabled to false, restart, and join to see that the welcome stops.
  • Run /setwelcome in game, then join again.

items.title: Quick reference
items.text:
These are the things you can do with config. Settings can hold text, numbers, or true and false.

Call What it does config.getValue(name) Gives back the value of a setting config.setDefault(name, value) Creates a setting, but only if it doesn't exist yet config.set(name, value) Changes a setting to a new value config.clear(name) Removes a setting and saves the file config.save() Writes your changes to config.yml config.setAutosave(true) Saves automatically every time you use set or setDefault, so you can skip config.save()

Next up is saving data.

items.title: Events
items.text:
Events are how your plugin reacts to things that happen in the game. You've already used two, PlayerJoinEvent and PlayerQuitEvent. In this lesson you'll learn how to see what an event gives you and how to cancel one so the thing never happens, and you'll finish with a plugin that protects certain blocks from being broken.

All the examples in this lesson use the same event, so replace the previous example each time instead of adding to it.

To see which events exist, check the event list, which has every event grouped by category.

items.title: Part 1: See what an event gives you
items.text:
When something happens in the game, Spigot makes an event that describes it and hands it to your function. Different events describe different things. A PlayerJoinEvent knows which player joined, and a BlockBreakEvent knows which player broke which block:

main.lua
plugin.registerEvent("BlockBreakEvent", function(event)
    local player = event:getPlayer()
    local block = event:getBlock()
    player:sendMessage("You broke: " .. block:getType():name())
end)

event:getPlayer() and event:getBlock() ask the event for the player and the block. Then block:getType() gives the kind of block it was, and :name() turns that into text like STONE or DIRT, so it can go in a message.

Every call here uses a colon, because the event and everything on it comes from Spigot.

Try it by breaking a few different blocks and reading what comes back.

items.title: Part 2: Cancel an event
items.text:
Events happen in two steps. First Minecraft says "this is about to happen", and your plugin gets to look at it. Then, if nobody stops it, it goes ahead. Calling event:setCancelled(true) is how you stop it:

main.lua
plugin.registerEvent("BlockBreakEvent", function(event)
    event:setCancelled(true)
    event:getPlayer():sendMessage("You can't break blocks here!")
end)

Now no block breaks, and the player gets a message instead.

This one stops everyone, including you

Once this is running, nobody can break any block. Take it out when you're done trying it.

Not every event can be cancelled. You can't cancel someone joining, for example, because it has already happened. The table at the end of this page shows which ones you can, and the event list shows it for every event.

items.title: Part 3: Only cancel certain blocks
items.text:
Stopping every block isn't very useful, so let's check which block it is first:

main.lua
plugin.registerEvent("BlockBreakEvent", function(event)
    local name = event:getBlock():getType():name()
    if name == "OBSIDIAN" then
        event:setCancelled(true)
        event:getPlayer():sendMessage("You can't break obsidian!")
    end
end)

That first line does a lot at once, so let's slow it down. Here is the same thing written as three separate steps:

main.lua
local block = event:getBlock()
local blockType = block:getType()
local name = blockType:name()
  • block is the block that was broken: one specific block in the world, sitting in one specific spot. If a player breaks two obsidian blocks, those are two different blocks.
  • blockType is what kind of block it is. Both of those obsidian blocks have the same type, which is obsidian. It isn't text, though. It's a Spigot object called a Material, so you can't compare it with a piece of text like "OBSIDIAN".
  • name is that type written out as text, like "OBSIDIAN". Now we have a piece of text, which is something we can compare.

Each : takes the answer from the step before and asks it the next question, so the one-line version is the same thing with the middle steps skipped. You'll see chains like this a lot in Spigot.

Next we use == to ask whether it's equal to "OBSIDIAN". A single = sets something, and a double == compares two things, so watch for that one. If it matches, we cancel the event and send the message, and any other block breaks as normal.

Block names are all capitals with underscores, like DIAMOND_BLOCK, and they have to match exactly. You can find every name in the Material list.

Names can change between versions

Many block names changed in Minecraft 1.13, so check the list for your server's version.

items.title: Putting it together
items.text:
To protect more than one block, use or. Replace your plugin's block event with this:

main.lua
plugin.registerEvent("BlockBreakEvent", function(event)
    local name = event:getBlock():getType():name()
    if name == "OBSIDIAN" or name == "DIAMOND_BLOCK" then
        event:setCancelled(true)
        event:getPlayer():sendMessage("You can't break " .. name .. "!")
    end
end)

or means either one is enough, so the event is cancelled for obsidian or for diamond blocks. The message includes the block's name, so the player knows what they tried to break.

Try these in survival mode:

  • Break a dirt or stone block, and it breaks as normal.
  • Break obsidian, and it stays put with a message.
  • Break a diamond block, and the same thing happens.

items.title: Quick reference
items.text:
These are some of the most-used events. Call things on them with a colon, like event:getPlayer(). Click an event's name to see its whole category, or open the event list to browse them all. Any Spigot event works, not just these.

Event When it happens Can you cancel it? Useful calls PlayerJoinEvent A player joins No getPlayer() PlayerQuitEvent A player leaves No getPlayer() PlayerDeathEvent A player dies No getEntity() PlayerInteractEvent A player clicks or uses something Yes getPlayer(), getItem(), getClickedBlock() PlayerMoveEvent A player moves, which happens very often Yes getPlayer(), getFrom(), getTo() PlayerDropItemEvent A player drops an item Yes getPlayer(), getItemDrop() PlayerCommandPreprocessEvent A player types a command, just before it runs Yes getPlayer(), getMessage() BlockBreakEvent A player breaks a block Yes getPlayer(), getBlock() BlockPlaceEvent A player places a block Yes getPlayer(), getBlock() EntityDamageEvent Anything takes damage Yes getEntity(), getDamage(), getCause() EntityDamageByEntityEvent Something is hurt by something else Yes getEntity(), getDamager(), getDamage() EntityDeathEvent A mob or other entity dies No getEntity() InventoryClickEvent Someone clicks in an inventory Yes getWhoClicked(), getCurrentItem(), getSlot()

Names must be exact

Event names are case sensitive, so PlayerJoinEvent works and playerjoinevent doesn't. If LuaCord can't find an event by its short name, try its full class name instead, like org.bukkit.event.player.PlayerJoinEvent.

Next up is messages and colors.

items.title: Messages and colors
items.text: You've been sending plain messages so far, which works, but a bit of color makes them much easier to read. In this lesson you'll learn how to add color to a message and how to send one to everyone on the server, and you'll finish with an /announce command that broadcasts a colorful message.

items.title: Part 1: Add color to a message
items.text:
Minecraft colors text with a special symbol, §, followed by a letter or number. For example §6 makes text gold and §c makes it red. That symbol is awkward to type, so most plugins let you write & instead and swap it afterwards. Put this helper at the very top of your main.lua, followed by a command that uses it:

main.lua
local function color(text)
    return (text:gsub("&", "\194\167"))
end

plugin.addCommand({
    name = "colors",
    description = "Show some colors",
    usage = "/colors"
}, function(event)
    local sender = event.getSender()
    sender:sendMessage(color("&6Gold &cRed &aGreen &9Blue &lBold &rNormal"))
end)

The color function takes some text and swaps every & for the § symbol. That swapping is what gsub does: text:gsub("a", "b") replaces every a in text with b. You'll use it again in the config lesson. The odd-looking \194\167 is just how Lua writes that symbol, so it works no matter how your file is saved. You don't need to understand how it works, just paste it at the top and use it anywhere. Then color("&6Gold ...") turns &6 into a real color code, and sender:sendMessage sends the result.

You can type the symbol yourself

If you'd rather skip the helper, typing § straight into your message works too, like sender:sendMessage("§6Hello"). Just make sure your file is saved as UTF-8, which VS Code does by default, or the symbol can come out garbled.

The codes work from left to right, so a color stays on until the next one changes it. &l makes text bold and &r resets everything back to normal. The table at the end of this page lists them all.

Try /colors and see which colors show up.

items.title: Part 2: Send a message to everyone
items.text:
sender:sendMessage only reaches one person. To reach everyone on the server, ask the server to broadcast it:

main.lua
plugin.addCommand({
    name = "wave",
    description = "Wave at everyone",
    usage = "/wave"
}, function(event)
    local sender = event.getSender()
    plugin.getServer():broadcastMessage(color("&e" .. sender:getName() .. " &7waves at everyone!"))
end)

plugin.getServer() gives you the server, and :broadcastMessage(...) sends a message to every player. Here we build the message from pieces, joining them with the two dots you saw earlier: a yellow &e, the sender's name, then a gray &7 for the rest. This command needs the color helper from Part 1 to be in your main.lua too.

Try /wave with another player online, and see that both of you get the message.

items.title: Part 3: Join the words together
items.text:
When someone types /announce Server restarts soon, each word lands in its own spot in the list of arguments. To send the whole thing as one message, you need to join them back together:

main.lua
plugin.addCommand({
    name = "announce",
    description = "Announce a message to everyone",
    usage = "/announce <message>",
    minArgs = 1
}, function(event)
    local args = event.getArgs()
    local message = table.concat(args, " ")
    plugin.getServer():broadcastMessage(color("&6[Announcement] &f" .. message))
end)

table.concat(args, " ") glues every word in the list together with a space between them, so Server, restarts and soon become Server restarts soon. We also set minArgs = 1 so that LuaCord complains if someone types /announce with nothing after it, like you saw in the Commands lesson.

items.title: Putting it together
items.text:
Combined, your main.lua looks like this:

main.lua
local function color(text)
    return (text:gsub("&", "\194\167"))
end

plugin.addCommand({
    name = "announce",
    description = "Announce a message to everyone",
    usage = "/announce <message>",
    minArgs = 1
}, function(event)
    local args = event.getArgs()
    local message = table.concat(args, " ")
    plugin.getServer():broadcastMessage(color("&6[Announcement] &f" .. message))
end)

The color helper runs on the whole message, so whoever uses the command can add their own colors. Try /announce &cThe server restarts in 5 minutes! and the text will come out red.

items.text:

items.title: Reading the Spigot docs
items.text: Spigot is far too big for any wiki to cover, so the most useful thing you can learn is how to look things up yourself. In this lesson you'll learn to find a method in the Spigot docs, read what it needs, and turn it into Lua, and you'll finish by writing a command with a method you found on your own.

items.title: Part 1: Find the docs
items.text:
The Spigot docs are a website that lists everything your plugin can do, and you can find it here. The people who make Spigot call these pages the Javadocs, since they're built from Java code.

Everything in the docs is grouped into packages, which are like folders, and every page shows its package at the top. The Player type is in the package org.bukkit.entity. Player events, like PlayerJoinEvent, are in org.bukkit.event.player. A few important things, like GameMode, are in org.bukkit. You don't need to memorize any of that, because the search box finds things for you.

Try it now. Open the docs and type Player into the search box at the top right. The results are grouped, and the packages come first, so the highlighted top result is the package for player events, which isn't the page you want. Scroll down to Classes and Interfaces and click Player, the one that says it's an interface in the package org.bukkit.entity. If you'd rather skip the search, here's the direct link.

At the top of that page is a short description and a line called "All Superinterfaces", which we'll come back to in Part 3. Further down is the Method Summary, a table with one row for every method. A method is something you can call, like player:sendMessage(...). You'll see some tabs above the table, but you can ignore those for now.

On the left side, just under the top bar, there's a Contents box with a search of its own. The search box at the top right looks through all of the docs, but this one only looks at the page you're on. Type part of a method's name into it, like walk, and the list below narrows down to the matching methods. Click one to jump straight to it. On a long page like this one, that's the quickest way to find a method.

items.title: Part 2: Read a method
items.text:
Every row in the Method Summary has three columns: a type on the left, the method in the middle, and a description on the right. Here are four real rows from the Player page:

Left column Middle column Description String getName() Gets the player's name int getLevel() Gets the player's experience level boolean getAllowFlight() Checks whether the player can fly by double-tapping jump void chat(String msg) Makes the player say something in chat

You read every row the same way. The left column is what you get back. The middle column is the method's name, followed by brackets, and whatever is inside the brackets is what you have to give it. Empty brackets mean you give it nothing, and (String msg) means you give it some text, where msg is just a label.

So the first row says "getName needs nothing and gives you text", and the last row says "chat needs some text and gives you nothing". In Lua, those four look like this:

local name = player:getName()           -- gives back text
local level = player:getLevel()         -- gives back a number
local canFly = player:getAllowFlight()  -- gives back true or false
player:chat("Hello!")                   -- needs text, gives back nothing

Anything after -- is a comment. Lua ignores it, so it's a good place to leave notes for yourself. When a method gives you something back, you can save it with local, and when it needs something, you put it between the brackets.

The left column uses Java's names for things, so here's what they mean in Lua:

Java type In Lua String Text, like "Hello" boolean true or false int, long A whole number double, float Any number, like 0.4 void Nothing comes back Anything else, like Location A Spigot thing. You get it from another call, or you import it.

Now let's use those same four methods in a command:

main.lua
plugin.addCommand({
    name = "stats",
    description = "Show some facts about you",
    usage = "/stats"
}, function(event)
    local sender = event.getSender()

    if event.isPlayerSender() then
        sender:sendMessage("Name: " .. sender:getName())
        sender:sendMessage("Level: " .. sender:getLevel())
        sender:sendMessage("Can fly: " .. tostring(sender:getAllowFlight()))
        sender:chat("I just checked my stats!")
    else
        sender:sendMessage("Only players can use this command.")
    end
end)

Text and numbers join straight onto a message with ... A true or false can't, so tostring turns it into text first.

When the left column isn't one of the simple types, like Location, it's a Spigot thing, and in the docs it's a link. Click it, and you land on its own page with its own list of methods. Following links like this is how you find your way around, and it's how we found getBlockX() in the last lesson.

items.title: Part 3: Where did the method go?
items.text:
Now try something that trips up almost everyone. Go back to the Player page and look for setHealth. It isn't in the Method Summary.

That's because a player is also a living thing, and a living thing is an entity, so Player gets many of its methods from the types above it. Those methods aren't listed in the main table. Instead, further down the page, you'll find sections called "Methods inherited from..." with a list of names under each one.

Search the page for setHealth and you'll find it under Damageable, which is one of those parent types. Click it, and you land on the Damageable page, where it's described in full. The top of the Player page also has a line called "All Superinterfaces", which lists every parent type, so you know where to look.

Can't find a method?

Search the page with your browser's find tool (Ctrl+F), and scroll down to "Methods inherited from". If it isn't there either, it may live on a different type, so try the search box on the docs site.

items.title: Part 4: When a method wants a Spigot thing
items.text:
Sometimes a method asks for something that isn't text or a number. For example, here's the line for changing a game mode:

void setGameMode(GameMode mode)

It wants a GameMode, which is a Spigot thing, and you can't get one from a player. This is where import comes in. Click GameMode in the docs, and the top of its page tells you its package, which is org.bukkit. You use that to bring it into your plugin:

main.lua
local GameMode = import("org.bukkit.GameMode")

plugin.addCommand({
    name = "creative",
    description = "Switch to creative mode",
    usage = "/creative"
}, function(event)
    local sender = event.getSender()

    if event.isPlayerSender() then
        sender:setGameMode(GameMode.CREATIVE)
        sender:sendMessage("You are now in creative mode.")
    else
        sender:sendMessage("Only players can change their game mode.")
    end
end)

import takes the package and the name, joined with a dot, and gives you the thing so you can use it. Names are case sensitive, so GameMode works and gamemode doesn't. As a shortcut, $ stands for org.bukkit, so import("$.GameMode") does the same job.

The page for GameMode also lists its values, which you'll find under "Enum Constants". That's where CREATIVE, SURVIVAL and the others come from. They have a dot, like GameMode.CREATIVE, because they're values you read, not methods you call.

If the name is wrong

If import can't find what you asked for, it gives you nothing, and an error appears in the server console. Check the package and the spelling.

You only need import when a method asks for a Spigot thing that you can't get from something you already have. Most of the time you can just follow a call, like player:getLocation().

items.title: Part 5: Do it yourself
items.text:
Now you try one on your own. Make a /fast command that makes you walk faster. Open the Player page and see if you can find the method that does it.

Here are some hints, in case you get stuck:

  1. On the Player page, type walk into the Contents box on the left, and click the method that does what you want.
  2. Read its row, as in Part 2. What does it want to be given? Is it text, a number, or something else?
  3. Read its details to find out which numbers are allowed, and what the normal speed is. Then pick a bigger one.

Once you've had a go, here's one answer:

main.lua
plugin.addCommand({
    name = "fast",
    description = "Walk faster",
    usage = "/fast"
}, function(event)
    local sender = event.getSender()

    if event.isPlayerSender() then
        sender:setWalkSpeed(0.4)
        sender:sendMessage("You walk faster now!")
    else
        sender:sendMessage("Only players can walk faster.")
    end
end)

The method is void setWalkSpeed(float value). It wants a number from -1 to 1, and anything outside that range causes an error. It gives nothing back, and the normal speed is 0.2, so 0.4 is double. Try it, and then try making a /normal command that puts it back.

items.text:
• The Spigot docs, where you can search for anything
  • Player, everything a player can do
  • Damageable, where setHealth lives
  • The event list, which lists every event you can listen to

Next up is config files.

items.title: Saving data
items.text:
Config files are for settings that the server owner changes. Saving data is for things your plugin remembers by itself, like how many times each player has joined. In this lesson you'll learn how to open a data file, save and load values, and update old saved data when your plugin changes. You'll finish with a plugin that counts every player's joins and remembers them after a restart.

Config and storage

A file you read and write from your plugin is called a storage object, and it works a lot like config, but the names are a bit different. config has setDefault, set and clear, and a storage object has setDefaultValue, setValue and clearValue. Also, config is called with a dot, like config.set(...), while a storage object is called with a colon, like data:setValue(...).

A storage object can open any YAML file, so you can also use one for an extra config file, like messages.yml. Just don't open config.yml that way, because config already looks after it.

items.title: Part 1: Save and read a value
items.text:
To store something, first open a file. Add this to your main.lua:

main.lua
local data = plugin.getStorageObject("data.yml")

plugin.registerEvent("PlayerJoinEvent", function(event)
    local total = data:getValue("total-joins") or 0
    total = total + 1

    data:setValue("total-joins", total)
    data:save()

    event:getPlayer():sendMessage("The server has had " .. total .. " joins!")
end)

plugin.getStorageObject("data.yml") opens a file called data.yml in your plugin's folder, and creates it if it isn't there yet. The ending of the name matters. Use .yml, which is easy to read and edit.

data:getValue("total-joins") reads a value. The first time, nothing has been saved yet, so it gives back nil. That's what or 0 is for: it means "use the saved number, and if there's nothing saved, use 0". It only picks a fallback for that one line and doesn't save anything. The saving happens afterwards, with setValue and save. Then we add one, and data:setValue stores the new number. That only changes it in memory, so data:save() writes it to the file. Without save, the number is lost when the server restarts.

Try joining a few times and then look at plugins/YourPluginName/data.yml.

items.title: Part 2: Save data for each player
items.text:
One counter for the whole server isn't very useful, so let's give every player their own. To tell players apart we use their unique ID, which never changes, even if they change their name. Replace your join event with this:

main.lua
local data = plugin.getStorageObject("data.yml")

plugin.registerEvent("PlayerJoinEvent", function(event)
    local player = event:getPlayer()
    local key = "joins." .. tostring(player:getUniqueId())
    local joins = (data:getValue(key) or 0) + 1

    data:setValue(key, joins)
    data:save()

    player:sendMessage("Welcome back, " .. player:getName() .. "! This is join number " .. joins .. ".")
end)

Here's what each line does:

  • local player = event:getPlayer() is the player who just joined.
  • local key = ... makes the label that this player's count is saved under. Every player needs their own label, so we build one from their unique ID, a long code like 0b2f4c1e-... that belongs to one player forever. tostring turns the ID into text, so it can be glued onto "joins.", which gives a label like joins.0b2f4c1e-.... The dot groups every player's count under one joins: heading in the file.
  • local joins = (data:getValue(key) or 0) + 1 works out the new count. It reads this player's saved count, or 0 if they've never joined, and then adds one. So the first time it's 0 + 1, which is 1, and the next time it's 1 + 1, which is 2. The brackets make sure the reading happens before the + 1.
  • data:setValue(key, joins) remembers the new count, and data:save() writes it to the file.
  • The last line sends the player a message with their count.

Join a few times and check that the number goes up, then restart the server and join again to see that it remembers.

items.title: Part 3: Look up and remove data
items.text:
Let's add two commands. The first shows your count, and the second resets it. Add them below the join event:

main.lua
plugin.addCommand({
    name = "joins",
    description = "See how many times you have joined",
    usage = "/joins"
}, function(event)
    local sender = event.getSender()

    if event.isPlayerSender() then
        local key = "joins." .. tostring(sender:getUniqueId())
        local joins = data:getValue(key) or 0
        sender:sendMessage("You have joined " .. joins .. " time(s).")
    else
        sender:sendMessage("Only players have a join count.")
    end
end)

plugin.addCommand({
    name = "resetjoins",
    description = "Reset your join count",
    usage = "/resetjoins"
}, function(event)
    local sender = event.getSender()

    if event.isPlayerSender() then
        local key = "joins." .. tostring(sender:getUniqueId())
        local removed = data:clearValue(key)

        if removed then
            data:save()
            sender:sendMessage("Your join count was reset.")
        else
            sender:sendMessage("You didn't have a join count to reset.")
        end
    else
        sender:sendMessage("Only players have a join count.")
    end
end)

Both commands start by making the player's key, the same way as in the join event, and /joins uses it to read the count. /resetjoins uses data:clearValue(key), which removes the saved count and tells you whether there was one to remove. It gives back true if it removed something and false if there was nothing there. We save that answer as removed, and the if uses it to pick the right message.

If you want to check a value without reading it, data:exists(key) gives back true or false.

items.title: Part 4: Update old data
items.text:
Just like with config, your plugin will change, and the data players have already built up shouldn't be lost. Saved data you read with or, like (data:getValue(key) or 0), already copes with something that's new, because an old file simply doesn't have it yet and the or supplies a starting value.

Moving data takes a bit more. Say version 1 of your plugin saved the server count as total-joins, and version 2 wants it under stats.total-joins. Add this near the top of your main.lua, right after you open the file:

main.lua
local data = plugin.getStorageObject("data.yml")

-- Version 2 moved "total-joins" to "stats.total-joins"
if (data:getValue("data-version") or 1) < 2 then
    local old = data:getValue("total-joins")
    if old then
        data:setValue("stats.total-joins", old)
        data:clearValue("total-joins")
    end
    data:setValue("data-version", 2)
    data:save()
end

Old data has no data-version, so or 1 treats it as version 1, and it goes into the if. If the old total-joins value is there, we copy it to the new place and remove the old one. Then we mark the file as version 2 and save, so this only ever runs once. New data skips the copy, since there's nothing to move.

Unlike config.getValue, a storage object's getValue gives you a real nil when nothing is saved, so if old then works.

Next time you change the layout, bump the number and add another if below this one.

items.title: Putting it together
items.text:
Combined, your main.lua is a join counter that every player gets their own count in:

main.lua
local data = plugin.getStorageObject("data.yml")

plugin.registerEvent("PlayerJoinEvent", function(event)
    local player = event:getPlayer()
    local key = "joins." .. tostring(player:getUniqueId())
    local joins = (data:getValue(key) or 0) + 1

    data:setValue(key, joins)
    data:save()

    event:setJoinMessage(player:getName() .. " joined the game! (join number " .. joins .. ")")
end)

plugin.addCommand({
    name = "joins",
    description = "See how many times you have joined",
    usage = "/joins"
}, function(event)
    local sender = event.getSender()

    if event.isPlayerSender() then
        local key = "joins." .. tostring(sender:getUniqueId())
        local joins = data:getValue(key) or 0
        sender:sendMessage("You have joined " .. joins .. " time(s).")
    else
        sender:sendMessage("Only players have a join count.")
    end
end)

plugin.addCommand({
    name = "resetjoins",
    description = "Reset your join count",
    usage = "/resetjoins"
}, function(event)
    local sender = event.getSender()

    if event.isPlayerSender() then
        local key = "joins." .. tostring(sender:getUniqueId())
        local removed = data:clearValue(key)

        if removed then
            data:save()
            sender:sendMessage("Your join count was reset.")
        else
            sender:sendMessage("You didn't have a join count to reset.")
        end
    else
        sender:sendMessage("Only players have a join count.")
    end
end)

One thing changed in the join event. Instead of sending a message to just that player, event:setJoinMessage(...) changes the message everyone sees when someone joins, so the server announces "Steve joined the game! (join number 3)".

Try these:

  • Join the server a few times and watch the number go up.
  • Restart the server and join again, and the count carries on.
  • Type /joins to see your count.
  • Type /resetjoins, then /joins to see it start from zero.

items.title: Quick reference
items.text:
These are the things you can do with a storage object. Call them with a colon, like data:save(). Values can be text, numbers, true or false, or tables.

Call What it does plugin.getStorageObject(file) Opens a .yml file in your plugin's folder, and creates it if it isn't there data:getValue(name) Gives back a saved value, or nil if nothing is saved data:setValue(name, value) Changes a value, which isn't written to the file until you save data:setDefaultValue(name, value) Sets a value only if it's missing, and gives back true if it did data:exists(name) Gives back true if something is saved there data:clearValue(name) Removes a value, and gives back true if there was one data:save() Writes your changes to the file

That's the end of Basics for now. You now know how to make commands, react to events, send colorful messages, work with players, read the Spigot docs, and keep settings and data. More is coming in Advanced.

items.title: Working with players
items.text: Most plugins end up doing something to players, like checking where they are or moving them around. In this lesson you'll learn how to read things about a player and how to change them, and you'll finish with a few handy admin commands.

items.title: Part 1: Read things about a player
items.text:
You already know how to find a player by name. Once you have one, you can ask them all sorts of questions. This command tells you where someone is:

main.lua
plugin.addCommand({
    name = "whereis",
    description = "Show where a player is",
    usage = "/whereis <player>",
    minArgs = 1,
    maxArgs = 1
}, function(event)
    local sender = event.getSender()
    local args = event.getArgs()
    local target = plugin.getServer():getPlayer(args[1])

    if target then
        local location = target:getLocation()
        sender:sendMessage(target:getName() .. " is at " .. location:getBlockX() .. ", " .. location:getBlockY() .. ", " .. location:getBlockZ())
    else
        sender:sendMessage("That player isn't online.")
    end
end)

target:getLocation() gives you the player's position, and then getBlockX(), getBlockY() and getBlockZ() give you its three coordinates as whole numbers. Lua happily joins numbers and text with .., so the message comes out like Steve is at 120, 64, -35.

Try /whereis with your own name and compare it with the coordinates on your screen.

items.title: Part 2: Change a player's game mode
items.text:
Some things you change need a bit of Minecraft's own vocabulary, like the game modes. To use them, you first bring them into your plugin with import:

main.lua
local GameMode = import("$.GameMode")

local modes = {
    survival = GameMode.SURVIVAL,
    creative = GameMode.CREATIVE,
    adventure = GameMode.ADVENTURE,
    spectator = GameMode.SPECTATOR
}

plugin.addCommand({
    name = "gm",
    description = "Change your game mode",
    usage = "/gm <survival|creative|adventure|spectator>",
    permission = "admintools.gm",
    minArgs = 1,
    maxArgs = 1
}, function(event)
    local sender = event.getSender()
    local args = event.getArgs()
    local mode = modes[string.lower(args[1])]

    if not event.isPlayerSender() then
        sender:sendMessage("Only players can change their game mode.")
    elseif mode then
        sender:setGameMode(mode)
        sender:sendMessage("Your game mode is now " .. string.lower(args[1]) .. ".")
    else
        sender:sendMessage("Pick survival, creative, adventure or spectator.")
    end
end)

import("$.GameMode") brings in Spigot's GameMode, which holds the four modes. The $ is a shortcut that stands for org.bukkit, where Spigot keeps it. GameMode.CREATIVE has a dot because it's a value you read, not a method you call.

The modes table lines up what the player types with the real game mode, so modes["creative"] gives you GameMode.CREATIVE. If they type something that isn't in the table, like /gm banana, the answer is nil. We use string.lower so Creative and CREATIVE work too.

The if has three outcomes: the console can't have a game mode, a valid mode changes yours, and anything else gets a hint. That's why we didn't need return here.

The permission line means only players with that permission can use the command, which keeps regular players from making themselves creative. Server operators can use it, and you can give it to others with a permissions plugin.

Try /gm creative and then /gm survival.

items.title: Part 3: Teleport players
items.text:
Teleporting works by handing a location to teleport. Here are two commands that use it. The first sends you to the world's spawn point:

main.lua
plugin.addCommand({
    name = "spawn",
    description = "Go to the world's spawn point",
    usage = "/spawn"
}, function(event)
    local sender = event.getSender()

    if event.isPlayerSender() then
        local spawnPoint = sender:getWorld():getSpawnLocation()
        sender:teleport(spawnPoint)
        sender:sendMessage("Teleported to spawn!")
    else
        sender:sendMessage("Only players can teleport.")
    end
end)

sender:getWorld() is the world you're in, :getSpawnLocation() is where that world's spawn point is, and sender:teleport(spawnPoint) moves you there.

The second brings another player to you:

main.lua
plugin.addCommand({
    name = "bring",
    description = "Teleport a player to you",
    usage = "/bring <player>",
    permission = "admintools.bring",
    minArgs = 1,
    maxArgs = 1
}, function(event)
    local sender = event.getSender()
    local args = event.getArgs()
    local target = plugin.getServer():getPlayer(args[1])

    if not event.isPlayerSender() then
        sender:sendMessage("Only players can use this command.")
    elseif target then
        target:teleport(sender:getLocation())
        sender:sendMessage("Brought " .. target:getName() .. " to you.")
    else
        sender:sendMessage("That player isn't online.")
    end
end)

This time we find the target with getPlayer, then target:teleport(sender:getLocation()) sends them to wherever you're standing.

Try /spawn, and with a friend online, /bring their name.

items.title: Pick a code editor
items.text:
Before you can write a plugin you need somewhere to write it, and a code editor is the right tool for the job. Two good free choices are Visual Studio Code and Notepad++. VS Code works on any system and colors your code so mistakes are easier to spot, and you can add Lua and YAML support by searching for them in its Extensions tab. Notepad++ is lighter and opens faster, but it's Windows only. Either one is fine, so use whichever you like.

Windows can hide the real file name

Windows often hides file extensions, so a file you named main.lua can quietly end up as main.lua.txt, and then your plugin won't load. To avoid this, turn on File name extensions in the View menu of File Explorer, then check that your files really end in .lua and .yml.

Once you have an editor, you're ready to make your first plugin.

items.title: Your first plugin
items.text: In this lesson you'll make a plugin that prints a message when it starts, adds a /hello command, and welcomes players when they join. We'll build it one piece at a time, then put it all together at the end.

items.title: 1. Make the folder
items.text: In your server's plugins folder, create a folder named exactly MyPlugin.lkt. The .lkt ending is how LuaCord knows the folder is a plugin.

items.title: 2. Add plugin.yml
items.text:
Inside that folder, create a file called plugin.yml, which tells LuaCord about your plugin:

plugin.yml
name: MyPlugin
version: "1.0"
main: main.lua
author: YourName
description: My first LuaCord plugin

The name and version are what they sound like, main is the Lua file that runs first, and author and description are there for anyone reading about your plugin.

items.title: 3. Write main.lua
items.text: Now create main.lua in the same folder. This is where your plugin's code goes, and we'll write it in three parts.

items.title: Part 1: Run something when the plugin starts
items.text:
Start your main.lua with this:

main.lua
plugin.onEnable(function()
    logger.info("My plugin is enabled!")
end)

plugin is just plugin related stuff. plugin.onEnable lets you say "run this when my plugin starts". You hand it a function, and LuaCord runs that function once, when the server turns your plugin on. Inside it, logger.info prints a message to the console, which is an easy way to see that your plugin is alive. Later on, this is also a good place to set things up before players arrive.

items.title: Part 2: Add a command
items.text:
Now add this below it:

main.lua
plugin.addCommand({
    name = "hello",
    description = "Say hello!",
    usage = "/hello"
}, function(event)
    local sender = event.getSender()
    sender:sendMessage("Hello from Lua!")
end)

plugin.addCommand takes two things. The first is a table that describes your command: name is what players type after the slash, description says what it does, and usage is how to use it. The second is a function that runs every time someone uses the command.

That function receives an event, which holds the details of who ran the command. You can name it anything you like, event is just a common choice.

Inside the function, the first line, local sender = event.getSender(), asks the event who ran the command and saves the answer as sender. The second line, sender:sendMessage("Hello from Lua!"), sends that person a message, which is why they see "Hello from Lua!" in chat.

Give every command a description

LuaCord only registers commands that have a description, so without one the command silently won't exist.

Dot or colon?

Things that come from Minecraft, like sender, are called with a colon, as in sender:sendMessage(...). If you use a dot on them you'll get an error like bad argument: userdata expected.

items.title: Part 3: Welcome players when they join
items.text:
Finally, add this at the bottom:

main.lua
plugin.registerEvent("PlayerJoinEvent", function(event)
    local player = event:getPlayer()
    player:sendMessage("Welcome to the server!")
end)

An event is something that happens in the game, and plugin.registerEvent lets you react to it. The first part is the name of the event, here PlayerJoinEvent, which happens whenever a player joins. The function runs every time it does.

This time the event comes from Minecraft and describes what just happened. event:getPlayer() gives you the player who joined, and player:sendMessage(...) greets them. Because both come from Minecraft, they use a colon.

items.title: Putting it together
items.text:
Combined, your main.lua looks like this:

main.lua
plugin.onEnable(function()
    logger.info("My plugin is enabled!")
end)

plugin.addCommand({
    name = "hello",
    description = "Say hello!",
    usage = "/hello"
}, function(event)
    local sender = event.getSender()
    sender:sendMessage("Hello from Lua!")
end)

plugin.registerEvent("PlayerJoinEvent", function(event)
    local player = event:getPlayer()
    player:sendMessage("Welcome to the server!")
end)

And your folder should look like this:

plugins/
└── MyPlugin.lkt/
    ├── main.lua
    └── plugin.yml

items.title: 4. Try it
items.text:
Restart the server and you should see "My plugin is enabled!" in the console. Join the server and you'll get "Welcome to the server!", and typing /hello in game replies with "Hello from Lua!".

Changed your code?

On a folder plugin you can run /luacord dev reload myplugin to reload it without restarting the server.

When you want to share the plugin as a single file, the next step is to pack it as a .lkt.

items.title: Download and install
items.text:
You need a Spigot or Paper server and Java 8 or newer. Download the latest LuaCord .jar from CurseForge or Modrinth, drop it into your server's plugins folder, and start or restart the server. That's all the setup there is.

To check that it worked, watch the console while the server starts. You should see these two lines:

Loading LuaCord plugins...
No LuaCord plugins were loaded.

The "no plugins" part is expected, since you haven't made one yet. That's what the next few pages are for, starting with picking a code editor.

items.title: Pack it as a .jar
items.text:
Sites like CurseForge and Modrinth only accept .jar files, so LuaCord has a free tool that wraps your .lkt into one. Make your plugin a .lkt file first, then open the JAR generator, upload your .lkt, fill in the details, and download the .jar. The generator runs in your browser, so your files never leave your computer.

Besides letting you upload to CurseForge or Modrinth, a .jar shows up in the server's /plugins list, which a plain .lkt doesn't. You use it like any other plugin by putting it in the plugins folder, as long as LuaCord is installed too.

That's the end of Getting Started. Next up are a few small plugins to help you get the hang of it.

items.title: Pack it as a .lkt file
items.text:
A .lkt file is your plugin folder squeezed into a single file, which makes it much easier to share, and it's also what you'll need for the .jar on the next page.

To make one, open your MyPlugin.lkt folder and select the files inside it (main.lua and plugin.yml), not the folder itself. Make them into a zip file, then rename the zip to MyPlugin.lkt.

Before you put it in your plugins folder, move the old MyPlugin.lkt folder out of there, onto your desktop for example. A folder and a file can't have the same name in the same place, so only one of them can be in plugins.

Files inside, not the folder

If you zip the folder itself, main.lua ends up one level too deep and the plugin won't load. Open the zip and check that main.lua is right at the top.

With your .lkt ready, you can turn it into a .jar.

items.title: Getting the hang of it
items.text:
You've made your first plugin, so now it's time to practice. The six plugins in this section are all small, and each one reuses what you already know and adds just one new thing. By the end, the same few shapes will start to look familiar.

Every page gives you the code for one plugin. You can add each one to the bottom of the main.lua you already have, so your plugin keeps growing, because each command and event works on its own. After you change your code, restart the server, or run /luacord dev reload myplugin to reload it without restarting.

  1. /heal fills your health bar.
  2. /feed fills your hunger bar.
  3. /fly turns flying on and off.
  4. /rules sends the server rules.
  5. A welcome with the player's name greets people by name when they join.
  6. A leave message prints to the console when someone leaves.

When you're done, you'll put them all together into one plugin you can share.

Start with /heal.

items.title: Putting it all together
items.text:
You now have six small plugins, so let's turn them into one plugin that's ready to share. Make a new folder called MyServerTools and put two files in it.

plugin.yml
name: MyServerTools
version: "1.0"
main: main.lua
author: YourName
description: Heal, feed, fly, rules and join and leave messages
main.lua
plugin.addCommand({
    name = "heal",
    description = "Heal yourself",
    usage = "/heal"
}, function(event)
    local player = event.getSender()
    player:setHealth(20)
    player:sendMessage("Healed!")
end)

plugin.addCommand({
    name = "feed",
    description = "Fill your hunger bar",
    usage = "/feed"
}, function(event)
    local player = event.getSender()
    player:setFoodLevel(20)
    player:sendMessage("Fed!")
end)

plugin.addCommand({
    name = "fly",
    description = "Toggle flying",
    usage = "/fly"
}, function(event)
    local player = event.getSender()
    local canFly = not player:getAllowFlight()
    player:setAllowFlight(canFly)
    if canFly then
        player:sendMessage("Flying is on! Double-tap space to fly.")
    else
        player:sendMessage("Flying is off.")
    end
end)

plugin.addCommand({
    name = "rules",
    description = "Show the server rules",
    usage = "/rules"
}, function(event)
    local sender = event.getSender()
    sender:sendMessage("Server rules:")
    sender:sendMessage("1. Be kind to everyone.")
    sender:sendMessage("2. No griefing.")
    sender:sendMessage("3. Have fun!")
end)

plugin.registerEvent("PlayerJoinEvent", function(event)
    local player = event:getPlayer()
    player:sendMessage("Welcome, " .. player:getName() .. "!")
end)

plugin.registerEvent("PlayerQuitEvent", function(event)
    local player = event:getPlayer()
    logger.info(player:getName() .. " left the server.")
end)

That's every plugin from this section in one file. Each command and event works on its own, so they all fit together without any changes.

items.title: Share it
items.text:
To turn it into something you can share, select main.lua and plugin.yml, make them into a zip file, and rename it to MyServerTools.lkt, just like on the .lkt page. Then upload that file to the JAR generator and download your .jar.

That's the end of Getting the hang of it. Next up is Basics.

items.title: /feed
items.text:
This plugin adds a /feed command that fills your hunger bar.

main.lua
plugin.addCommand({
    name = "feed",
    description = "Fill your hunger bar",
    usage = "/feed"
}, function(event)
    local player = event.getSender()
    player:setFoodLevel(20)
    player:sendMessage("Fed!")
end)

items.title: How it works
items.text: This is almost a copy of /heal, and that's the point. A lot of plugins are the same pattern with a different method: get the player, do something to them, and send a message. Here the method is setFoodLevel(20), where 20 is a full hunger bar. Once you notice the pattern, you'll start seeing it everywhere.

items.title: Try it
items.text:
Wait until your hunger bar drops a bit, then type /feed. Like /heal, it needs a player to run it.

Next: /fly.

items.title: /fly
items.text:
This plugin adds a /fly command that turns flying on and off each time you use it.

main.lua
plugin.addCommand({
    name = "fly",
    description = "Toggle flying",
    usage = "/fly"
}, function(event)
    local player = event.getSender()
    local canFly = not player:getAllowFlight()
    player:setAllowFlight(canFly)
    if canFly then
        player:sendMessage("Flying is on! Double-tap space to fly.")
    else
        player:sendMessage("Flying is off.")
    end
end)

items.title: How it works
items.text:
player:getAllowFlight() asks whether the player is allowed to fly right now, and the answer is either true or false. Putting not in front of it flips the answer, so true becomes false and the other way around, and we save that as canFly. Then player:setAllowFlight(canFly) applies it, which is why the command works as a switch.

The if part picks a message to send. If canFly is true the first message runs, and otherwise the one after else runs.

Try it in survival

In Creative mode you can always fly, so you won't notice a difference there. In Survival, type /fly and then double-tap the space bar.

Next: /rules.

items.title: /heal
items.text:
This plugin adds a /heal command that fills your health bar. It's your first command that changes something about the player instead of just sending a message.

main.lua
plugin.addCommand({
    name = "heal",
    description = "Heal yourself",
    usage = "/heal"
}, function(event)
    local player = event.getSender()
    player:setHealth(20)
    player:sendMessage("Healed!")
end)

items.title: How it works
items.text:
The command is set up exactly like /hello, and the only new part is player:setHealth(20). setHealth is a method that comes from Minecraft, so it's called with a colon, and 20 is a full health bar, since each heart is worth 2. We also named the variable player this time instead of sender, which shows that the name is up to you, so pick whatever makes your code easiest to read.

Run it as a player

/heal only works when a player runs it. The console isn't a player, so it has no health to fill.

items.title: Try it
items.text:
Take some damage, then type /heal and watch your hearts fill back up.

Next: /feed.

items.title: A welcome with the player's name
items.text:
This plugin welcomes each player by name when they join, like "Welcome, Steve!".

main.lua
plugin.registerEvent("PlayerJoinEvent", function(event)
    local player = event:getPlayer()
    player:sendMessage("Welcome, " .. player:getName() .. "!")
end)
path: A welcome with the player's name

items.title: How it works
items.text:
This is the join event from your first plugin, with one change to the message. player:getName() gives you the player's name, and the two dots .. glue pieces of text together, so "Welcome, " and the name and "!" become one message.

How did we know about getName?

It comes from the Spigot API documentation, and soon you'll learn how to look up methods like this yourself.

Next: a leave message.
path: A welcome with the player's name

items.title: A leave message
items.text:
This plugin prints a message in the console whenever a player leaves.

main.lua
plugin.registerEvent("PlayerQuitEvent", function(event)
    local player = event:getPlayer()
    logger.info(player:getName() .. " left the server.")
end)

items.title: How it works
items.text:
It looks just like the join event, only with a different event name: PlayerQuitEvent happens when a player leaves. Events come in all kinds, and they all work the same way, so learning one teaches you the rest.

This time we use logger.info instead of sendMessage. The player has already left, so there's nobody to send a message to, and the console is the place to see it.

items.title: Try it
items.text:
Join your server, leave, and look at the console for your name.

That's all six. Next, put them all together into one plugin.

items.title: /rules
items.text:
This plugin adds a /rules command that shows your server's rules.

main.lua
plugin.addCommand({
    name = "rules",
    description = "Show the server rules",
    usage = "/rules"
}, function(event)
    local sender = event.getSender()
    sender:sendMessage("Server rules:")
    sender:sendMessage("1. Be kind to everyone.")
    sender:sendMessage("2. No griefing.")
    sender:sendMessage("3. Have fun!")
end)

items.title: How it works
items.text:
Nothing is new here except that sendMessage is called more than once. Each call shows up as its own line in chat, so you can send as many lines as you like. Change the text to your own rules and you've got a real command for your server. It also works from the console, since it only sends messages.

Next: a welcome with the player's name.
